newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK money supply points to prices pressure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK money supply points to prices pressure.

text.p: British money supply grew strongly last month, which coming on top of a dramatic drop in jobless numbers and good retail sales, shows the economy is powering ahead and interest rates might have to rise soon.
The Bank of England reported on Thursday that M4 money supply -- a possible indicator of future inflation -- rose 10.8 percent in the year to November, while bank lending also surged.

The central bank said M4, a broad measure which comprises notes and coins in circulation, personal and commercial bank deposits and certificates of deposit, grew a provisional seasonally-adjusted 1.1 percent in November from October.
This brought the year-on-year rate to 10.8 percent compared with 10.3 percent in October, well above the upper limit of the government's three to nine percent monitoring range.

"With lending to the private sector also growing strongly, the Bank of England is likely to continue to highlight the rapid growth of broad money supply in pressing for further rises in interest rates in the new year," said Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke bowed to pressure from the central bank in October and raised official interest rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent.

The Conservative government, which lost its overall majority in parliament last week, is anxious to avoid raising rates before a general election which must be held by next May as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of people.
The opposition Labour Party has a strong lead in opinion polls.

Nevertheless, many economists believe Clarke may have to bite the bullet and order another interest rate rise at his next monetary policy meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on January 15.
The big drop in jobless numbers released on Wednesday and strong retail sales growth, were seen adding to the pressure on Clarke.
The British Bankers' Association said total sterling lending by major banks rose 4.556 billion pounds ($7.62 billion) in November.
"The major banks' lending in November was driven by demand from across the economic sectors," said the association's director-general Tim Sweeney.

Separate figures from the Building Societies Association (BSA) showed net new home loan approvals slipped to 3.651 billion pounds in November from 3.967 billion in October, but the underlying trend remained firm.
The housing market is a key barometer of economic confidence in this nation of home-owners.

"The slight fall in lending in November is not a sign of a faltering recovery but rather that it is more stable and likely to be sustainable in the longer term," BSA director-general Adrian Coles said.
"This is good news for the economy and the housing and mortgage markets."

M4 was seen in the late 1980s as a reliable pointer to future inflationary pressures but, in recent years, it has been distorted by special factors such as mergers and acquisitions in the financial sector.
November M4 lending was again swollen by heavy corporate borrowing which is not seen as carrying the same inflation threat as lending to the personal sector.

"Nevertheless, the personal sector itself posted another large increase consistent with strong retail sales in the month, and is probably indicative of more to come," said Jeremy Hawkins, an economist at Bank of America.
